parts.title: Part 1. Complete the text. Each missing word appears somewhere else in the text.
parts.text: When I moved into a student flat last year, I could not cook anything except eggs. For the first month I ate in cheap cafes, but soon I had no money left. My grandmother gave me a small book of family recipes, and I decided to try one recipe every week. The first {{1}} I tried was plov, and it was a disaster: the rice was hard and the meat was burnt. I called my grandmother, and she explained that I had used too much heat. The second time, the {{2}} was soft and the meat was perfect. Since then I have learned to make soup, salads and two kinds of bread. Cooking at home is much cheaper than eating in {{3}}, and it is also healthier. My flatmates now share the {{4}} for food, and in return I cook dinner for everyone on Sundays. Last month my {{5}} visited us and tasted my plov. She said it was almost as good as hers. Now I am the one who teaches my friends how to {{6}}.

parts.title: Part 2. Read the article and choose the correct answer.
parts.text:
When Rano Alimova decided to learn to drive at the age of sixty-one, her children thought she was joking. She had spent her whole life in the passenger seat, first beside her father and later beside her husband, and she had never felt the need to take the wheel herself. Everything changed when her husband's eyesight began to fail. 'Suddenly the person who drove us everywhere couldn't do it any more,' she says. 'Either I learned, or we stayed at home.'

Her first lessons were, by her own account, frightening. Traffic in the city had become much heavier since her youth, and she found it difficult to watch the mirrors, the road and the instructor's hands at the same time. Several times she considered giving up. What kept her going, she says, was her instructor, a patient young man who never raised his voice and who suggested they practise early on Sunday mornings, when the roads were almost empty.

Rano failed her first driving test because she drove too slowly on the main road. She was disappointed but not discouraged. 'At my age, you know that mistakes are not the end of the world,' she explains. She passed at the second attempt, three months later.

Today she drives her husband to his appointments and visits her grandchildren in a nearby town every weekend. She has also become something of a local celebrity: two of her neighbours, both women in their fifties, have started lessons with the same instructor. 'They saw that I could do it,' Rano says, 'so they stopped making excuses.'

questions.prompt: Why did Rano decide to learn to drive?

options.text: She wanted to find a job.
Her husband could no longer drive.
She had always dreamed of driving.

questions.prompt: What did Rano find most difficult in her first lessons?

options.text: Paying attention to several things at once.

questions.prompt: Why did the instructor suggest Sunday mornings?
Why did Rano fail her first test?

options.text: She forgot to check the mirrors.

questions.prompt: How did Rano react to failing?

options.text: She stopped her lessons for a year.
She stayed positive and tried again.

questions.prompt: What effect has Rano had on her neighbours?

options.text: They think she is too old to drive.
They have started learning to drive.

parts.title: Part 3. Choose the best heading for each paragraph. There are two headings you do not need.

paragraphs.text: Most food waste begins in the shop, not the kitchen. People buy what looks good or what is on special offer, then discover at home that they have no plan for it. Spending ten minutes on Sunday deciding what you will cook during the week, and writing a list based on that, can cut waste dramatically.

Many products carry two different dates. A 'use by' date is about safety and should be taken seriously, especially for meat and dairy products. A 'best before' date, however, only tells you when the quality may start to decline. Rice or biscuits a day or two past that date are usually perfectly fine to eat.

Where you keep food matters as much as when you eat it. Tomatoes and bananas lose flavour in the fridge, while fresh herbs last much longer if you put them in a glass of water. Keeping older items at the front of the shelf also means you are more likely to use them first.

Yesterday's rice can become today's fried rice, and vegetables that are starting to soften are ideal for soup. Many traditional dishes around the world were originally invented as ways of using what was left from an earlier meal, so there is nothing second-class about cooking this way.

Sometimes you simply have more than your family can eat, for example after a celebration. Instead of throwing it away, offer it to neighbours, or use local community groups that connect people who have extra food with those who need it.

Some waste cannot be avoided: vegetable peel, tea leaves, eggshells. If you have a garden or even a balcony, letting this material break down returns nutrients to the soil and reduces the amount of rubbish sent to landfill.

parts.title: Part 4. Read the text and choose the correct answer.
parts.text:
Few workplace ideas have spread as quickly in recent years as the four-day week. Trials in several countries have reported impressive results: employees working thirty-two hours instead of forty, with no loss of pay, said they were less stressed and slept better, while many employers found that productivity held steady or even rose. To its supporters, the case seems almost closed.

Economists, however, tend to be more cautious, and their reservations deserve attention. The first concerns the trials themselves. Companies that volunteer to take part are usually those whose managers already believe the idea will work, and whose work can be reorganised relatively easily. An advertising agency that cuts unnecessary meetings is a very different proposition from a hospital, a school or a bus company, where services must be provided every day and fewer hours per person simply means hiring more people.

A second concern is what happens after the novelty wears off. Employees who know they are part of a high-profile experiment may work unusually hard to prove that it succeeds. Whether the same gains can be sustained over five or ten years, when the arrangement has become ordinary, is still largely unknown.

None of this means the idea is without merit. Even sceptics accept that much office work contains a great deal of wasted time, and that a shorter week can force organisations to identify and remove it. The more interesting question may not be whether the four-day week works, but for whom. A policy that suits software developers may be unworkable for nurses, and imposing one model on every sector would risk creating new inequalities between workers who can benefit and those who cannot.

Perhaps the most realistic outcome is a gradual one. Rather than a single national change, we may see a patchwork of arrangements: four-day weeks in some industries, flexible hours in others, and in some sectors very little change at all. That may disappoint campaigners who hoped for a revolution, but it would reflect the very different realities of modern work.

questions.prompt: What does the first paragraph say about the trials?
Why does the writer mention a hospital and a bus company?

options.text: To show that they took part in trials.
To show where a shorter week is hardest to introduce.

questions.prompt: What is the problem with companies that volunteer for trials?

options.text: Their managers already expect the idea to work.

questions.prompt: What does 'after the novelty wears off' refer to?

options.text: When the arrangement is no longer new and special.

questions.prompt: According to the writer, what do even sceptics accept?

options.text: Much office work involves wasted time.

questions.prompt: Which outcome does the writer consider most likely?

parts.title: Part 2. Listen to a phone message. Complete the notes with ONE word or a number.
parts.script: Hello, this is Bekzod calling from the Brightway Training Centre about your application for the evening web design course. I'm happy to tell you that there's still a place for you. The course starts on Monday the fourteenth and runs for ten weeks. Classes are on Mondays and Wednesdays from half past six to nine in the evening, in room twenty-two on the third floor. You'll need to bring your own laptop; if that's a problem, we can lend you one, but please tell us in advance. The fee can be paid in two parts: half before the course starts and half after five weeks. On the first evening there's a short test, just so the teacher can see what you already know, so don't worry about it. Please confirm your place by Friday, either by phone or by replying to our email. If we don't hear from you, we'll offer the place to someone on the waiting list. Thanks, and have a good day.

parts.title: Part 3. Listen to two colleagues discussing a team trip. Choose the correct answer.
parts.script:
Aziz: Have you seen the email about the team trip in May?
Lola: Yes. The manager wants us to choose between a weekend in Khiva and a day trip to the mountains.
Aziz: Khiva sounds amazing. I've never been.
Lola: It does, but think about the travel. It's a long journey, and half the team has small children. A whole weekend away is difficult for them.
Aziz: I hadn't thought of that. Still, a day in the mountains is just a long walk. We could do that any time.
Lola: Not really. The plan includes a guide who'll teach us about the plants and the history of the area, and there's lunch at a guesthouse. It's more than a walk.
Aziz: Okay, that sounds better. What about people who don't like hiking? Rustam hurt his knee last month.
Lola: The email says there's a shorter route along the river. He could take that and meet us for lunch.
Aziz: Fair enough. So you'll vote for the mountains?
Lola: I think so. Though if Khiva were closer, I'd choose it without hesitating.
Aziz: Maybe we could suggest Khiva for the autumn, as a longer trip with families invited.
Lola: That's a great idea. Let's put it in our reply.

questions.prompt: What are the two options for the trip?
Why does Lola have doubts about Khiva?

options.text: It is hard for colleagues with young children.

questions.prompt: What makes the mountain trip more than a walk?

options.text: A guide and lunch at a guesthouse.

questions.prompt: What could Rustam do?
How does Lola feel about Khiva?

options.text: She would choose it if it were closer.

questions.prompt: What do they decide to suggest?

options.text: An autumn trip to Khiva with families.

parts.title: Part 4. Listen to a short talk. Choose the correct answer.
parts.script:
Over the past two decades, many schools have reduced the time spent teaching handwriting, on the reasonable assumption that most adult writing now happens on keyboards. It's a shift that seems sensible, but a growing body of research suggests we may want to be more careful about what we give up.
The central finding is fairly consistent. When students take lecture notes by hand, they tend to remember the content better than students who type, even though typists usually record more words. The leading explanation is that handwriting is slow. Because you cannot write down everything, you are forced to decide what matters and put it into your own words, and that act of selection and rephrasing is itself a form of learning. Typists, by contrast, can copy almost word for word, which requires much less thought.
I'd add two qualifications. First, the advantage seems to depend on how the keyboard is used rather than on the keyboard itself. Students who are taught to summarise rather than copy while typing narrow the gap considerably. Second, for some learners, those with certain motor difficulties for instance, handwriting is so effortful that it gets in the way of thinking altogether, and for them a keyboard can be liberating.
So what should schools do? I'm not arguing for a return to hours of copying out letters. The skill worth protecting is not neat handwriting as such, but the habit of processing information actively. Handwriting happens to encourage that habit naturally, which is a good reason to keep it in classrooms, especially for note-taking. But the deeper goal should be to teach students how to listen, select and rephrase, whatever tool they happen to be holding.

questions.prompt: Why did many schools teach less handwriting?

options.text: Handwriting was thought to be harmful.
Most adults now write on keyboards.

questions.prompt: According to the research, why do handwritten notes help memory?

options.text: Writing slowly forces students to select and rephrase.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker's first qualification?

options.text: How the keyboard is used matters.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker mention learners with motor difficulties?

options.text: To argue for more handwriting practice.
To show that handwriting can be a barrier for some.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker think schools should protect?

options.text: The habit of processing information actively.

questions.prompt: Which best describes the speaker's position?

options.text: Handwriting is useful mainly because it encourages active learning.

Dear customer,

On 12 and 13 March, internet service in your area will be interrupted between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. while we upgrade our equipment. From April, the monthly price of the Home Plus plan will increase by 15%, but the speed will double. Please tell us how these changes affect you and whether you would like to move to a different plan.

CityNet Customer Service
